prologue.title: First Shift

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Night one — someone is about to need you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For half a second you're nine years old again — a corded phone, rain on the glass, a busy signal that never ends.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You know why you're here. You've always known.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A prank? You have to tell the difference.

decision.prompt: First night. What do you tell yourself?

choices.label: I'm here to help all of them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One call at a time.

prologue.synopsis: First night on the headset. A single flash of memory hints at why Charlie is here: a child, a phone, a busy signal.

plot_call.title: Week 1 — The Call That Drops

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A young woman has been kidnapped.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I'm at, a house on Calder's Street, Please I nee—

decision.prompt: The line just died. What do you do?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Straight to a dead tone — the line's been pulled.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Units roll on Calder Street. Sirens first, questions after. The house is empty — one shoe by the door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Calder Street. You grew up two doors down from that address.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Red lights passed your window once and kept going — to the wrong house. You never told anyone at the center.

plot_call.synopsis: A kidnapping call from Calder Street dies mid-sentence. Charlie grew up on that street. Callback or units — his first real choice.

weekend.title: After Hours

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Saturday. The shift is over.

decision.prompt: Alone with the pattern. What do you do?

choices.label: Start a private life — dates, go outside, everything.
I should focus on what happened.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You close the laptop, untie your necktie and pour a drink, you are Off Duty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You open a notebook and write down everything you remember.

weekend.synopsis: Saturday after the dropped call. Start a life outside the job, or start a notebook.

plot_call.title: Week 2 — The Voice

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A gruesome voice appears on the Line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A gruesome voice appears on the Line. All week you've told yourself the patrol you sent to Calder Street got there in time. The voice doesn't sound like it agrees.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A gruesome voice appears on the Line. It has the same quality as Calder Street's dead tone — a line someone pulled on purpose.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: This city will burn. And you can't stop us.

decision.prompt: A real tip. Your authority to dispatch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The car's already rolling. You'll write it up after.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You get it all down — times, cameras active, telephone antennas near possible locations.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The voice notices what you plot, and hangs up.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: One more thing, dispatcher. You sound like someone who's lost something. I collect that sound.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The line goes dead. Your coffee has gone cold around your hand.

plot_call.synopsis: A distorted voice promises the city will burn. It isn't a prank — it knows dispatch procedure. Report it, dispatch on it, or keep it talking.

plot_call.title: Week 3 — Vans at night

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A neighbor's whisper, hand cupped around the receiver.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A neighbor's whisper, hand cupped around the receiver. You've been keeping your own map of nights like this — Calder Street, the stadium — and it's starting to fill in.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Hello, this is Edward, I live on the 37th. Vans at 3am appear, I see them every once in a while near the stadium, they are here right now.

decision.prompt: A real tip. Your authority to dispatch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A unit rush towards the scene.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: License plates, vehicle details.

choices.label: File it the only way the system allows.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The unit reports a vehicle that was full of Stadium Merchandise.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The unit reports a vehicle full of Stadium Merchandise. Your Week 2 notes put the antennas near the stadium too. That's twice now — and twice is a pattern.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You open a case for your supervisor.

plot_call.synopsis: A neighbor reports vans by the stadium at 3am — the second stadium thread. Dispatch fast or build the record; the pattern starts to fill in.

plot_call.title: Week 4 — The Envelope

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: End of shift. There's an envelope tucked under your keyboard — cash.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: End of shift. There's an envelope tucked under your keyboard — cash. About the size of the installment you missed. Whoever left it did their homework.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: End of shift. There's an envelope tucked under your keyboard — cash. The exact kind your empty wallet has been dreaming about all week.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: End of shift. There's an envelope tucked under your keyboard — cash. Someone noticed the case file you've been building. This is what noticing costs them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: End of shift. There's an envelope tucked under your keyboard — cash. Enough for a real dinner at the corner café, and then some. That's the first thing you think of. That's exactly how they get you.

decision.prompt: An envelope of cash. Nobody saw it arrive.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody knows anything. No camera caught it. Turn it in, and you're telling the building something is going on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody knows anything. No camera caught it. You filed the vans away like the system wanted — maybe this is the system saying thank you.

decision.prompt: You understand the offer now — and that no one's hand is on it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You bag it, photograph it, log it. Your hands shake. Now there's paper that says someone paid you to look away — and you said no.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The cash goes in your jacket. Warm, heavy, easy. You just learned the price of looking away. So did whoever gave it to you.

plot_call.synopsis: An envelope of cash under the keyboard. Nobody saw it arrive. Log it and become a target, or pocket it and become a customer.

plot_call.title: Week 5 — Her Voice Again

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 2:57 a.m. A whisper call, road noise underneath — a phone hidden low, in a moving vehicle.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: You answered before. Calder Street. I remember your voice.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: Please don't hang up. They're in the front seat.

decision.prompt: It's her. Moving. Maybe four minutes of battery.

choices.label: Keep her talking — every detail is a map.
Ping the towers and triangulate now.
Run her audio through the analyzer.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: We stop where it echoes. Big and empty, like a... a stadium? There's a gate. Gate C.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Gate C. You write it on your skin because paper can be taken.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two towers catch her signal — both sit on the stadium district. Then the trace thins out to nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The analyzer isolates a sound under the road noise: a stadium PA test, same one every Tuesday night. District confirmed. Your case file gets its first hard edge.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: They're slowing down. If nobody comes, please just— remember I called. Last time nobody—

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Click. You sit with your hand on the dead line like it's a pulse.

decision.prompt: The line is gone. What do you leave her with?

choices.label: "I will find you." Say it like a fact.
Log everything. Promises are for amateurs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You say it to a dead line anyway. Some promises are for you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Times, sounds, Gate C. Cold ink, warm anger. The file is becoming a case.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nine years old. The dispatcher stayed on the line with you and the sirens still went to the wrong house.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That's why you don't hang up. Ever.

plot_call.synopsis: Mara — the Calder Street girl — calls from a moving vehicle. Stadium district confirmed. First origin memory plays: the sirens that went to the wrong house.

plot_call.title: Week 6 — The Audit

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A glass room, a folder, and a detective from Internal Affairs who pours you water you didn't ask for.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: Response logs on your shift have been edited after hours. 3 a.m., supervisor credentials, going back years.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: You're not accused. You're the only one whose numbers are clean. That makes you useful — or inconvenient.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: Response logs on your shift have been edited after hours. And one more thing keeps coming up: an envelope.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: You're sweating, dispatcher. Rooms like this notice.

decision.prompt: IA is watching you across the table. Play it how?

choices.label: Point at the pattern — vans, the stadium, the edits.
Ask for the raw, unedited logs — quietly.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: Stadium district. Same as the edits. You just connected my dots for me.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The detective slides you a card with a personal number. 'Not the switchboard. Ever.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You give the room nothing. The detective smiles like someone filing you under 'later.'

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: Raw logs. Off the record.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every edit traces to one supervisor login — older than your badge, still active. Someone senior never logged out of the past.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Back on the floor, the center hums like nothing happened. Somewhere in this building, a login is watching the watchers.

plot_call.synopsis: Internal Affairs pulls Charlie in: someone edits response logs at 3 a.m. with supervisor credentials. Cooperate, stonewall, or buy the raw logs. If he took the envelope, the room gets hot.

weekend.title: Coffee at 3 A.M.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The café for people with weird hours. Your partner stirs sugar into coffee that stopped being coffee an hour ago.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: Everyone signs one correction eventually. Times get smoothed, response looks better, the city sleeps.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: You sign, you go home. That's the whole religion around here.

decision.prompt: Your partner just confessed to one signature. Your move.

choices.label: Let it go. Protect the friendship.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A napkin, a case number from memory. Their hand shakes writing it. Now you owe each other silence — or the truth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You talk about anything else. The case number stays in their pocket, and between you.

weekend.synopsis: Weekend interlude: the partner admits everyone signs 'corrections.' Ask for proof or protect the friendship.

plot_call.title: Week 7 — The Wrong Address

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A house fire, a panicked caller, an address on the screen: 84 Harlow Drive. Units rolling.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: They're driving PAST us! The trucks — they went past! We're at FORTY-eight! Four-eight!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 84. 48. Two digits doing a little dance. You have seen this exact dance before — through a window, when you were nine.

decision.prompt: Protocol says verify, then re-route. The fire says now.

choices.label: Re-route on your own authority. Now.
Verify per protocol, then correct it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You call it. Trucks U-turn mid-block. Thirty seconds — that's what your childhood cost, and what you just gave back.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: They're here! They're HERE! Thank you—

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Verification takes ninety seconds. The family gets out; the kitchen doesn't. Nobody will ever write those ninety seconds up. You will remember them anyway.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Later you pull the original entry. The caller said forty-eight — clearly. Someone keyed 84. The correction was already drafted before you touched anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The 'errors' aren't errors. They're cover — traffic steered away from streets where certain vans work.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A photocopy you've owned since you were sixteen: response time, 4 minutes. Your memory: 9. Two numbers doing a little dance.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've been carrying a smoothed log your whole life. Tonight you learned they still make them.

plot_call.synopsis: A transposed address sends fire trucks the wrong way — the exact failure that killed Charlie's mother. He catches it live, then discovers the 'error' was pre-drafted. Second origin memory: the photocopied report.

plot_call.title: Week 8 — The Partner

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your partner drops a printout on your desk face-down, the way people hand over things they can't say.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: The login behind the edits — it's supervisor-level, older than both of us. Created before this building had cameras.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: Whoever owns it never logged out of the old system. Or the old habits.

decision.prompt: Your partner is halfway in. All the way is dangerous.

choices.label: Bring them in. Two sets of eyes.
Keep them out. This lands on you alone.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: Okay. We split shifts on watching the log. First edit we catch live, we screenshot everything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It stops being your case and starts being a case.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You take the printout and burn the copy trail. If this goes wrong, it goes wrong on one name: yours.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your personal phone buzzes. Unknown number. Nobody has this number.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: How's your mother, Charlie? Oh — my mistake. Old data.

decision.prompt: He just used your name. And hers.

choices.label: Say nothing. Let him hear silence.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You give him dead air — the one thing a voice can't stand. He hangs up first. Small victory. It counts.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: It was always personal, dispatcher. You just didn't know which person.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The line dies. The room feels colder by exactly one family.

plot_call.synopsis: The corrupted login is older than the staff. Recruit the partner or go alone — then The Voice calls Charlie's personal phone and mentions his mother by name.

plot_call.title: Week 9 — Two Alarms

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 11:58 p.m. A bus rollover downtown, twenty callers at once. And underneath the noise: a silent alarm — stadium warehouse, Gate C.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: Busy night, dispatcher. Bus full of people, or an empty old warehouse. Choose. That's the job, isn't it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He's on the line like he owns it. The screens don't disagree.

decision.prompt: Every unit you have, and one too few. Call it.

choices.label: Everything to the bus. People first, always.
Split coverage — bus heavy, one unit to Gate C.
Call in off-duty favors to cover both.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The bus empties into ambulances — everyone lives. At Gate C, cameras catch three vans leaving in convoy. Cargo unknown. He counted on your decency like it was a schedule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Bus scene holds — barely. The lone unit at Gate C radios in: 'Container row. You need to see this.' Then, quieter: 'Bolt cutters. Now.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Retired badges, off-shift medics, one tow-truck saint. The bus empties AND Gate C gets lit up like a match day. Some debts are worth owing.

lines.speaker: voice
lines.text: Interesting choice. I'll remember the shape of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So will you. Whatever happens at the stadium now happens on the map YOU drew tonight.

plot_call.synopsis: The Voice engineers a diversion: a mass-casualty bus crash against a silent alarm at Gate C. The allocation choice writes the finale: cargo moved, container found, or both scenes covered.

plot_call.title: Week 10 — The Raid

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Third call. No whisper this time — she's spent it all getting to a real phone.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: Stadium. Container row behind Gate C — blue containers, third one has a white door. There are nineteen of us.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: They load the vans on Sunday. You said you'd find me. Find me before Sunday.

decision.prompt: The system leaks. The clock runs. Route this how?

choices.label: Call the detective's personal line. Off the record.
File it by the book, but time-stamp everything publicly.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: Off the record gets warrants moving on the record. Saturday night. Tell no one inside your center — no one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For once, the leak springs on their side: nobody warns the vans.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You file it loud — copies everywhere, timestamps notarized by sheer volume. Too public to bury. The raid happens because burying it would now be the scandal.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Saturday, 11:40 p.m. Bolt cutters. Floodlights. A white door opens and the night inhales.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nineteen girls walk out blinking into the blue-red wash. One of them asks the officers: 'Which one of you is the voice?'

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: It's you, right? On the phone. It's you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They put her on the radio because she won't get in the ambulance until they do. You say her name. She says yours. The channel stays quiet for a moment out of respect.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The vans' paper trail dies inside city systems — permits, routes, corrections. Signed by a login you already know.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You saved nineteen. Now comes the man who made saving them this hard.

plot_call.synopsis: Mara's third call gives the exact container. Route around the leak — detective's personal line or aggressively public filing. The raid lands: nineteen rescued, and the paper trail points inside city systems.

plot_call.title: Week 11 — The Name on the Log

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The detective lays the edits out by date, oldest first. Then stops. Slides one page across, face-down — the way your partner did.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: The oldest smoothed log in the archive. Decades old. Same login.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: 48 Calder Street. Medical call. Logged response: four minutes. Actual: nine. Caller: a minor. A boy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You are nine years old. The dispatcher stays with you. The lights pass the window. Your mother's hand is in yours and then, at some point you refuse to remember exactly, it isn't.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Someone typed 4 over the 9 before the sun came up, and the center's numbers stayed beautiful.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: The login belongs to the night supervisor from back then. He never left the building, Charlie. He runs it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: R. HALE. The man who pinned your badge. The man who calls you 'son' in the hallway.

decision.prompt: Thirty years of smoothed nights, and one of them is yours.

choices.label: Confront Hale tonight, face to face.
Build it cold. Every log, every signature, no warning.
Pull the original archive box yourself first.

lines.speaker: director
lines.text: You were the boy on Calder Street? Then you know why the numbers matter. Panic doesn't fund a dispatch center, Charlie. Confidence does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He doesn't deny it. He explains it. Somehow that's worse.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You say nothing to him. You smile in the hallway. You photograph everything. The warmest thing about you now is the copier.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The archive box smells like a basement keeping secrets. Inside: the original tape. Your own nine-year-old voice, saying the address right. Twice.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You did nothing wrong. You've waited a lifetime for a cardboard box to say so.

plot_call.synopsis: The oldest falsified log is Charlie's mother's call — signed by the same login still editing today: Director Hale. Full origin memory plays. Confront him hot, build the case cold, or pull the archive tape.

weekend.title: The Night Before

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You don't sleep. The folder sits on the table like a guest who won't leave.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You don't sleep, but you don't sit alone either. They put their hand flat on the folder — not to open it. Just so it isn't only yours all night.

decision.prompt: Tomorrow has one shape or another. Tonight, choose yours.

choices.label: Call your mother's old number. Let it ring once.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: By 4 a.m. the speech is clean, short, unanswerable. Like a good dispatch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Disconnected, of course. You let it ring once anyway. 'One call at a time,' you tell the dial tone, and finally sleep.

weekend.synopsis: The night before the end: rehearse, or ring a disconnected number once. If love is high, someone stays.

plot_call.title: Week 12 — The Last Shift

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: City Hall, a long table, microphones with red lights. The center's numbers on a projector — beautiful, like always. You know what beauty costs now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: City Hall, a long table, microphones. Somewhere in Hale's desk is an envelope logged against YOUR name — his leash on you. Today you find out what it's made of.

lines.speaker: director
lines.text: Before you speak, son — centers run on trust. Break this one and every caller hears it in every voice on every line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He believes it. That was never the question.

decision.prompt: The microphone is warm. The city is listening.

choices.label: Testify. All of it — the logs, the vans, Calder Street.
Take the quiet deal: he retires, the victims' fund gets everything.
Testify — including about the envelope. About you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You read the numbers the way he never let them be read: nine, not four. Nineteen, not zero. Hale falls the way institutions fall — slowly, then all at once.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The center gets rebuilt with glass walls. Recruits learn Calder Street by name.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He retires 'for health reasons.' The victims' fund is enormous and permanently anonymous. The log stays smooth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Except one. At 3 a.m., supervisor credentials open one old record and correct it the other way: response time, 9 minutes. Some corrections go toward the truth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You testify about the edits, the vans — and the envelope in your jacket that night. The room goes very quiet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It costs you the badge. It buys you the mirror. Hale falls with you, and only one of you lands clean.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Months later. A call routes to you like it knows the way.

lines.speaker: mara
lines.text: Hey. It's not an emergency. I start college Monday. I just wanted the voice to know.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You watch the city lights hold steady. One call at a time.

plot_call.synopsis: Finale: hearing room. Testify and topple Hale, take the quiet deal and secretly correct one log, or confess the envelope too and fall clean. Coda: Mara calls — not an emergency, just a life continuing.

library.title: A man fell from a 2nd floor!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A small crowd, a man on the pavement, a phone shaking in someone's hand.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: A man fell from a 2nd floor! He's not moving much!

choices.label: Is he breathing? Don't move him.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: He's breathing but groaning. We didn't touch him.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: We're at 14 Almond Court, by the bakery.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Paramedics get there fast. He'll keep his spine and his bad luck. The city exhales.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A roar, then an impact you can feel through the phone. Car alarms, screaming, a voice shouting from the middle of the street, out of breath.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Oh my god — a plane just hit the tower!

choices.label: Are you clear of the falling debris?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Small plane, I'm not sure, I'm across the river!

choices.label: Stay Safe. I'm tracking your location.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Okay — thank you very much, pls hurry!

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Fire crews and rescue rolling, ambulances right behind. Keep everyone back across the street — you gave them a clear scene to work.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A gentle crunch of plastic, followed by the loudest human being in the city.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Emergency! A guy crashed into me!

choices.label: Sir, was it you who crashed?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Nobody's hurt! BUT he won't give me his insurance. The nerve!

choices.label: Leaving the scene — get a plate, stay safe.
Block him with your cart. Citizen's arrest 🛒
I'll log it. Don't chase him.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Plate's BUN-2-GO. We're at Maple and 5th. Send someone… and maybe some fries.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Patrol's rolling for the hit-and-run report. Bumper's fine, ego's totaled.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A kitchen, a hiss you can almost hear through the line, a very nervous caller.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: HELP, it smells like gas in here!

choices.label: Don't flip any switches. Get outside now.
Light a match, see what happens.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Okay, okay, I'm going out. The whole hallway reeks.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Apartment 3B, 88 Renner Street.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Crew shuts the main and airs it out before a spark finds it. Quietly heroic.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A wet cough rattles down the line.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: HELP! I'm coughing really bad! 😷

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I... ate glass. It was a challenge!

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Don't scare me! Just send help! 4 Maple Ave.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Ambulance dispatched. You talk them calm until it arrives.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A panicked voice, drowning in numbers.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I can't pay my debt! 💸

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: My student loan! They said I'm too young to work.

choices.label: Run away before it's too late! 😏

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I'm 12! What do I do?!

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Go back to your toys, kiddo. And free the line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A dim alley. Something small shuffles between the trash cans. The caller is not breathing easy.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I found a baby dinosaur!

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: That's what I thought too. Until now.

choices.label: Let's say I believe you… what breed?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: No, it's a baby! I think it's a T-REX. Maybe?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: 18th, Jurassic St.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: 18th, Jurassic St.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: You send Dino Control. The jeep rolls out — only unit trained for a baby T-Rex.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Background music. A hiccup. The slow, careful voice of someone who thinks they're being very clear.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Hi… is this 911? I just wanted to say… you guys are doing a GREAT job. *hic* Truly.

choices.label: Sir, are you having an emergency?
Thank you. How many fingers am I holding up?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Emergency? Noooo. Well — they're out of nachos. That FEELS like an emergency. But no.

choices.label: Drink water. Don't drive. Call a friend.
I'll send a unit… of pizza. Now hang up.
Please keep this line free for emergencies.

lines.speaker: caller

library.title: She's Not Breathing

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Medics take over a crying, breathing baby. You unclench one finger at a time. Best save of the month — and it was made of counting out loud.

library.synopsis: CPR coached down the line, beat by beat, until the baby cries. The emotional heavyweight of the daily rotation.

library.synopsis: A kid on a patched walkie reports a missing friend at the quarry — sweet, eerie, and ultimately explainable. Probably.

library.synopsis: Severance-flavored: an office worker trapped in a basement 'retreat' where the exit is a myth. Creepy-funny.

library.title: Handcuffed to a Billboard

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Wind noise, traffic far below, and a man speaking with the confidence of someone whose plan is still — technically — in progress.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Okay, first: this is a marketing activation. Second: I'm handcuffed to the billboard on Route 9. Third: the key is in my other pants.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: The pants are with my business partner. Who is also my ex-wife. Who is not answering. The billboard says 'ESCAPE ROOMS — YOU'LL NEVER WANT TO LEAVE.'

choices.label: Ladder unit's coming. Don't wave at traffic.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Tell them to bring bolt cutters and maybe a sandwich. The irony up here is very filling but not, like, food.

lines.speaker: dispatch
lines.text: Ladder crew frees one entrepreneur, forty feet up, zero regrets. The escape room gets its best review ever: 'Couldn't leave. Five stars.'

library.synopsis: A guerrilla-marketing stunt gone exactly as wrong as it sounds. Better Call Saul energy, forty feet up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Off the clock. First badge in your pocket that says DISPATCHER. The title is small. The way people start looking at it isn't.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The ones who used to talk over you, who never bothered to learn your name — they hear what you do now, and something behind their eyes shifts. This kind of respect doesn't get handed to you. You answer for it, one call at a time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You don't say much. You don't have to. The badge doesn't need announcing — and for the first time, walking your own street, you don't shrink.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You hold your head up. Let them look. You spent years being overlooked; tonight you take up your full size, and nobody argues.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Senior Dispatcher now. Word gets around a small city. A save you worked makes the local news — a voice on the line that kept someone here long enough for help to arrive.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The people who used to wave off the job — 'you just answer phones' — go quiet when it comes up now. They're starting to understand that the phone is the first thing that stands between a bad day and a funeral.

decision.prompt: The doubters are reconsidering. What sits with you?

choices.label: It's not about them. It's about whoever calls next.
Feels good to be seen for once.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Either way, the story travels further than you do. You go back to the board the next night the same as always — but the city's picture of you has quietly changed.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Supervisor stripes. The job stops being an abstraction to the people around you the day an emergency lands on a street you know — and the calm voice that walked someone through it came from a room like yours.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The ones who used to mock the work don't have jokes anymore. When it's their block, their worst minute, the person on the other end of the line is suddenly the most important voice in the world. They get it now.

decision.prompt: Respect earned the hard way. How do you meet it?

choices.label: Graciously. Everyone's someone's worst day eventually.
Let the work keep answering for you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No speeches, no I-told-you-so. Just the quiet arithmetic of a city learning what you're for. The doubt doesn't survive contact with a real emergency.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Commander. The higher you go, the heavier the nights. The calls you carry home now are the ones nobody else could hold. Respect at this rank isn't given — it's the residue of everything you didn't let fall apart.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The people who once thought this was easy work will never know the weight of a bad night on the board. That's the trade: they respect the title, and you carry what earns it in silence.

decision.prompt: The weight is real. How do you hold it?

choices.label: Set it down for the night. You did enough today.
Carry it. It's the price of being the one they trust.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You breathe. Tomorrow the board lights up again, and again you'll be the steady voice at the center of someone's chaos. That's not a job title anymore. It's who you became.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Chief Operator. A room at City Hall, your name read out loud with the word 'service' after it. Somewhere in the folding chairs sit people who once looked right through you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There's no version of this where they don't have to admit it now. The ones who doubted, who mocked, who never expected anything of you — they're clapping. Respect, finally, out loud and on the record.

decision.prompt: The recognition you never expected. What do you feel?

choices.label: Grateful. And a little proud. You allow yourself that.
Focused. The medal doesn't answer calls — you do.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You take the applause, then you take the elevator back down to the floor. The praise is nice. The work is the point. But tonight, just for a moment, the room feels a little bigger.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Director of the center. Now there are new recruits who look at you the way you once looked at the people who seemed untouchable. The doubt that used to follow you has been replaced by something else entirely: aspiration.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The ones who mocked the job are the ones telling the next generation to learn from you. Full circle — from overlooked to the standard other people measure themselves against. You earned this desk one call at a time.

decision.prompt: What do you pass on to the ones just starting?

choices.label: Stay on the line when everyone else would hang up.
Be the calm voice in someone's worst minute. That's the whole job.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They hang on the words. Respect isn't something you chase anymore — it's the room you walk into. And it all started with picking up a phone nobody thought mattered.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The café near the station, the one open at weird hours for people with weird hours. Someone at the counter is reading the book you own two copies of.

lines.speaker: stranger
lines.text: They always burn the espresso here. We keep coming anyway.

choices.label: Nod politely and take your cup to go.

lines.speaker: stranger
lines.text: Okay, burnt espresso tastes better free.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You trade a smile and a phone number scribbled on a napkin. The walk home feels shorter.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Twenty minutes about the book, the city, the espresso. No numbers exchanged — but this café has weird hours, and so do you both.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You take the cup and the exit. Through the window, the reader turns a page. Maybe next time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Final installment of the semester's plan. One more payment and the university lets go of your collar for a while.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A notice on your door. The yellow kind. Pay what's owed by Friday, or the apartment stops being yours. The hallway pretends it didn't read it. It read it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Final installment. You have the money — you've had it since the envelope. It spends like any other money. You tell yourself that twice.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: PAID — the semester's plan, closed. The apartment is yours, every scuffed square meter of it. You stand in the kitchen a while, just because you can.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: All of it, fees included. The account shows a zero so clean it looks fake. You screenshot it. Some trophies are just receipts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You box what matters in two trips. A friend's couch, for now. The city keeps calling all night anyway — it doesn't care where you sleep, only that you answer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The reminder goes off as you hang up your headset. First installment, due by midnight. The payment portal loads slower than any emergency line you've ever worked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Paid. The balance barely notices, but the apartment stays yours another month. You make coffee in it like a small ceremony.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The portal adds a late fee and a red banner. Somewhere in the fine print, the word 'lien' appears for the first time. It reads like a countdown.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Bills, flyers, and one envelope with the university's crest. You know before opening it: the student loan office found your new address.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Installments start this month. Miss them, and the lien lands on the one thing you own — the apartment.

choices.label: Pin it to the fridge. You'll make the payments.
Call and argue about the interest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The letter goes on the fridge, next to the shift schedule. Two pieces of paper that own your life now. You'll answer to both.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Forty minutes on hold to learn the interest is 'non-negotiable.' You're better on the other side of a phone line. The installments stand.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Second installment. The portal remembers you now — it greets you by your full legal name, the way nothing friendly ever does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Second installment — plus the one you missed, plus the late fee. The letters have stopped being polite. This one mentions the apartment by address.

choices.label: Skip it. The city pays badly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Paid. You eat cheap for a few days and tell yourself it's a diet. The apartment doesn't thank you. It doesn't have to — it stays.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Everything, plus fees. The red banner disappears. For one night, the account and your conscience are both clean, and the wallet is very, very light.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Skipped. The portal logs it without comment. Machines don't threaten — they schedule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two missed now. The next letter won't be a letter. It'll be a notice on the door — the yellow kind the whole hallway can read.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: First break of the shift. The vending machine hums, the microwave light flickers, and your stomach files a formal complaint.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bag of nuts from the vending machine. Not a meal, but your hands stop shaking halfway through the next call.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A real plate, hot food, ten quiet minutes. You walk back to the console feeling like a person again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Tap water in a paper cup. Free, cold, and loud in an empty stomach. The city doesn't care if you ate.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The napkin number turned into a dinner. Small place, candle in a bottle, the kind of nervous that feels good.

lines.speaker: date
lines.text: So a 911 operator. Do you ever get to say 'what's your emergency' in real life?

choices.label: 'You grab this one, I'll get the next.'

lines.speaker: date
lines.text: Smooth. Okay — next one's on me. And there WILL be a next one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You walk out lighter in the wallet and lighter everywhere else too.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Half and half, no fuss. 'Fair,' they say, approvingly. Somehow that lands better than a grand gesture.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Bold — assuming a second date.' They pay, smiling. On the sidewalk they say it: 'Tuesday works.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A call at an hour that's never good news. Your friend's voice is doing the thing yours does on the worst shifts — steady on purpose.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.text: I hate asking this. Rent's short this month. Twenty would save me until Friday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A call at an hour that's never good news. Your friend's voice is steady on purpose. So is yours — twenty is real money this week, and you both know what asking costs.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.text: I hate asking this. Rent's short this month. Twenty would save me until Friday.

decision.prompt: You know what it costs to ask.

choices.label: Send half and a home-cooked meal.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Sent. No lecture attached. The 'thank you' that comes back is three words long and heavier than it looks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Half the money and a full plate. You eat together on a Tuesday, and the rent stops being the point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You can't fix Friday, so you spend an hour on the phone fixing everything else. It's not twenty bucks. It's not nothing, either.

events.title: A Text From an Old Friend

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Shift's over. Your phone buzzes — a name you haven't seen since before the academy.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.text: Heard you're working the 911 lines now?? That's insane. Wanna catch up sometime?

decision.prompt: An old friend, out of nowhere.

choices.label: Yes! Grab a bite right now — my treat.
Leave it on read. Too tired.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two burgers, one hour, five years covered. The laugh is the same as ever. You'd forgotten what off-duty felt like.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Soon.' A thumbs up comes back. People say 'soon' a lot in this job. Some of them mean it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The message sits there, read and unanswered. The city takes your voice all night; sometimes there's none left over.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: First time they see your place. The couch has a dent shaped like your double shifts, and the fridge has… condiments.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: Okay, movie's picked. Food situation?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The good noodles arrive hot and the movie's forgettable, which is fine — the couch dent fits two.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: You made THIS out of three condiments and rice?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Dispatcher improvisation, kitchen edition. They ask for seconds. The movie never gets finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two bowls, extra butter, zero pretension. Halfway in they steal your bowl. You allow it. This is serious, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The group chat wakes up after months asleep. Someone found a taquería that's open late. Everyone's in. Everyone's asking about you.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.text: You in?? We're covering the table, everyone throws in for their share.

decision.prompt: First invite in a long time.

choices.label: Go, but just for a soda.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Tacos, bad jokes, someone's terrible karaoke. Nobody asks about the sirens. For three hours you're just a person at a table.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You nurse one soda and stay two hours anyway. Turns out the company was the thing, not the tacos.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The chat posts photos until 1 a.m. You sleep early, wake rested, and scroll through the night you didn't have.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One month since the burnt espresso. Same café, same weird hours. They're already at the counter, holding two cups, one of them yours.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: A month of putting up with dispatch schedules. I think that deserves something.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One month since the burnt espresso. They're already at the counter, holding two cups. You could buy out this whole café now. You liked it better when you couldn't.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: A month of putting up with dispatch schedules. I think that deserves something.

choices.label: Claim 'your' table by the window, forever.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The flower stand guy says 'the usual?' and you realize you've been planning this for a week. They carry the flowers all the way home like a trophy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You write 'RESERVED — weird hours only' on a napkin and prop it on the window table. The barista laminates it the next day. It's official, then.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: Two burnt espressos. To bad coffee and good timing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Paper cups touch like champagne glasses. Somewhere outside, a siren goes by — and for once, it's not yours to answer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Their birthday is Thursday. You've been staring at the same shop window for ten minutes: the nice edition of the book from the café, the one with the map inside the cover.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Their birthday is Thursday. The nice edition sits in the window, and for once you can afford it without checking your balance. You know exactly why — and you spend the whole walk there not thinking about it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Their birthday is Thursday. Money's been thin since you bagged that envelope and became the building's least popular honest person. The shop window doesn't care about integrity.

choices.label: Write them a letter. Just words.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Thursday: they unwrap it, freeze, and read the map inside the cover for a full minute before saying anything. Worth every shift it cost.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The napkin with the phone number, framed in cheap wood. They laugh, then don't. It goes on the wall by the door, where keys live — the important spot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A page and a half, in your careful report-writing hand, about weird hours and burnt espresso. They keep it in a jacket pocket. You catch them re-reading it twice.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Late. The city hums below the fire escape. You came home quiet again, and this time they didn't pretend not to notice.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: The job takes pieces of you some nights. Where do they go?

decision.prompt: Nobody's ever asked it like that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You talk until the streetlights buzz off. Voices you couldn't save, ones you did. They hold your coffee so your hands are free to shake. It helps. All of it helps.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It's the truest thing you've said all week, and you both know it. The city hums. Nobody moves for a long time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Fine.' The word every operator knows means the opposite. They let it go — this time — and the space between you keeps its exact width.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Second date, no restaurant this time — just the long way home through streets you usually only hear about through a headset.

lines.speaker: date
lines.text: You went quiet at that corner. Rough call once?

choices.label: Tell them the truth — a little of it.
Change the subject with a joke.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You tell it plainly, no drama. They don't flinch, don't pity — they just move a half step closer for the rest of the walk.

lines.speaker: date
lines.text: Deal. I collect long stories.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A promise shaped like a door left open.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The joke lands, the laugh is real, and the corner stays yours alone. Some walls take longer than others.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The two halves of your off-duty life at one table. The friends brought embarrassing stories. Your partner brought an appetite for them.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.text: Has this one told you about the academy fitness test yet? No? OH.

choices.label: Tell the story yourself — worse version.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Dinner's on me' buys exactly eleven seconds of mercy, then the story gets told anyway. Money well wasted. The table votes to keep your partner.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: You got stuck WHERE on the rope climb?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You tell it worse than it was, because that's what the table deserves. Two worlds, one laugh. It fits.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Slander,' you declare, as three phones produce photographic evidence. Your partner saves one for later. You're doomed, happily.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A number you don't know. When you pick up, the voice is careful, low — a detective, off the record.

lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: That case file you kept building? Somebody upstairs finally read it. We're moving. Quietly. I wanted you to hear it from me first.

decision.prompt: The thing you documented is becoming real. What do you say?

choices.label: Tell me what you need. I'm in.
Keep my name out of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You hand over everything — dates, plates, the map you kept on your fridge. For the first time the quiet on Calder Street has someone official listening.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Understood,' the detective says. Your name stays off it, but the file does the talking. Sometimes that's the bravest way to be brave.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: 'Yeah,' the detective says, not arguing. 'It did.' Then, quieter: 'Thanks for not letting it die.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A knock at your door you didn't order. The man on the other side doesn't introduce himself. He doesn't have to.

lines.speaker: stranger
lines.text: We appreciate a dispatcher who knows when to look away. Keep doing that. It'd be a shame if you forgot how.

decision.prompt: He's on your doorstep. What do you do?

choices.label: Close the door. Don't say a word.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You shut the door and stand behind it a long time. The message landed anyway. That was the point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He smiles like your words are cute. 'Sure you didn't.' The door clicks shut on his side, and the street is very quiet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You nod. He's gone before you finish. You just agreed to something without saying a single word — the cleanest kind of deal.
